# Overview

This tutorial accompanies "Missing Not at Random Models for Multilevel Analyses of Longitudinal and Intensive Longitudinal Data." The paper describes how to specify shared parameter and selection models for multilevel analyses of longitudinal change and intensive longitudinal data, and this document walks through every analysis in the paper with executable code and annotated output. The two documents are meant to be read together: the paper explains the models, and this tutorial explains the syntax. Section headings here follow the paper, so a reader can move from a paper section to the matching code, and the model numbers correspond to Tables 2 through 5 in the paper.

Every analysis is presented twice, as a Blimp script and as the equivalent `rblimp()` function call in R. The two specifications are identical: each Blimp command maps onto an `rblimp` argument of the same name, and both run the same Blimp computational engine and produce the same output. The one difference is graphics. The missingness-probability figures and model-implied trajectories in this tutorial are drawn with R plotting functions that operate on `rblimp` model objects, so those sections are R-only; everything else can be run from either interface.

**Software.** Blimp is a free download for macOS, Windows, and Linux from [https://www.appliedmissingdata.com/blimp](https://www.appliedmissingdata.com/blimp); rblimp is on CRAN (`install.packages("rblimp")`) and requires Blimp to be installed first. Two short documents in the repository cover the setup: the [Blimp Installation Guide](https://craigenders.github.io/mnar-mlm/Blimp-Installation-Guide.html) walks through installing Blimp, Blimp Studio, and rblimp on each platform, and the [Blimp Scripting Quick Start](https://craigenders.github.io/mnar-mlm/Blimp-Scripting-Quick-Start.html) introduces the scripting language and the correspondence between Blimp commands and `rblimp()` arguments. Readers new to Blimp should skim both before the [Blimp and rblimp](#blimp-and-rblimp) section below, which explains the specific commands this tutorial uses.

**Online materials.** The GitHub repository at [https://github.com/craigenders/mnar-mlm](https://github.com/craigenders/mnar-mlm) includes a PDF of the paper, the four example data sets (`data/`), the R scripts (`rblimp/`), the Blimp scripts (`blimp/`), this tutorial and the companion documents (`docs/`), including a document on the equivalence between dummy-coded missingness models and item response theory (IRT) missingness models.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Illustrative Data

The paper uses simulated data because no single real data set includes the full range of features that influence the specification of MNAR models. Two designs are crossed with two missing data patterns, giving four data sets.

| Data set | File | *N* | *T* | Design | Missingness |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--|
| Growth, dropout | `growth-dropout.csv` | 500 | 5 | Linear growth | Monotone attrition after baseline |
| Growth, intermittent | `growth-intermittent.csv` | 500 | 5 | Linear growth | Intermittent at every occasion |
| Intensive, dropout | `intensive-dropout.csv` | 125 | 20 | Stationary process with a time-varying covariate and heterogeneous variance | Monotone attrition after occasion 7 |
| Intensive, intermittent | `intensive-intermittent.csv` | 125 | 20 | Same | Intermittent at every occasion |

Each file has 2,500 rows in stacked (long) format, one row per person per occasion, with missing values coded `NA`.

| Variable | Definition | Data sets |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `l2id` | Person identifier (level-2 cluster) | All |
| `time` | Occasion index, coded 0, 1, ..., *T* -- 1 | All |
| `group` | Binary grouping variable (0/1), e.g., an intervention indicator | All |
| `y` | Outcome with missing values | All |
| `x` | Time-varying covariate with missing values | Intensive |

The growth model is a two-level linear growth curve with random intercepts and slopes, with `group` predicting both.

$$Y_{ti} = \alpha_i + \beta_i(\mathit{TIME}_{ti}) + \varepsilon_{ti}$$

The intensive repeated measures model regresses the outcome on a time-varying covariate centered at its latent person mean (so the slope reflects only within-person variation), with a random intercept, a random slope, and a random within-person log-variance $\omega_i$ (a location-scale model).

$$Y_{ti} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\left(X_{ti} - \mu_{Xi}\right) + \varepsilon_{ti} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\left(X^{w}_{ti}\right) + \varepsilon_{ti}$$

In both designs, the level-2 model includes a binary grouping variable that predicts the random intercepts and slopes.

$$\alpha_i = \gamma_{0\alpha} + \gamma_{1\alpha}(\mathit{GROUP}_i) + \zeta_{\alpha i} \qquad \beta_i = \gamma_{0\beta} + \gamma_{1\beta}(\mathit{GROUP}_i) + \zeta_{\beta i} \qquad \omega_i = \gamma_{0\omega} + \zeta_{\omega i}$$

Missingness was generated from a probit selection model in which time indicators, the grouping variable, random effects, and observed and unobserved outcome scores predicted nonresponse. The data-generation scripts are in the repository.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Blimp and rblimp

Each analysis below is shown twice: as a Blimp script and as the equivalent `rblimp()` function call in R. The two are interchangeable. A Blimp script is a plain-text file with a `.imp` extension in which major commands end with a colon and the specifications within each command end with a semicolon; `#` begins a comment. Each Blimp command becomes an argument of the same name to `rblimp()`. The `DATA` and `MISSING` commands have no counterpart because the data and missing value codes are already encoded in the R data frame. Text inputs such as variable lists and equations are quoted in R; numeric inputs are not.

| Blimp command | rblimp argument | Description |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `DATA` | `data` | Data file (Blimp) or R data frame (rblimp) |
| `MISSING` | --- | Missing value code (not needed in R) |
| `CLUSTERID` | `clusterid` | Level-2 identifier variable |
| `TIMEID` | `timeid` | Integer variable indexing repeated measurement occasions; required for lagged variables and for the `DROPOUT` command |
| `DROPOUT` | `dropout` | Creates the binary missingness or dropout indicator from an incomplete outcome |
| `LATENT` | `latent` | Defines level-2 latent variables (random effects) |
| `FIXED` | `fixed` | Declares completely observed predictors; speeds estimation by omitting their distributional models |
| `CENTER` | `center` | Latent group-mean centering for a level-1 predictor |
| `MODEL` | `model` | Focal model and missingness model regression equations |
| `PARAMETERS` | `parameters` | Derived quantities computed from model parameters at each iteration |
| `WALDTEST` | `waldtest` | Joint Wald test of a set of coefficients |
| `SEED` | `seed` | Random number seed |
| `BURN` | `burn` | Warm-up iterations per chain (discarded) |
| `ITER` | `iter` | Post-warm-up iterations used for parameter summaries |
| `NIMPS` | `nimps` | Number of imputed data sets to save (used for plotting predicted probabilities) |
| `CHAINS` | `chains` | Number of MCMC chains; the default of 4 is used throughout and the command is omitted |

Several features of Blimp's modeling language appear repeatedly and are explained the first time each is used:

- **Block labels** (`level2:`, `level1:`, `missingness:`) organize the `MODEL` command; they are optional and have no effect on estimation.
- **Parameter labels** (`intercept@g0a`) name a coefficient so it can be used in a `PARAMETERS` expression or a definition variable; **fixed values** (`intercept@-3`, `| intercept@0`) constrain a coefficient to a constant.
- **The vertical pipe** separates fixed effects (left) from random effects (right) in a level-1 equation. Blimp adds a random intercept to a multilevel model by default, so `| intercept` could be omitted; it is written explicitly throughout because the dropout models fix it to zero with `| intercept@0`.
- **Boolean expressions** such as `(time == 3)` evaluate to 1 or 0 and act as dummy codes on the right-hand side of an equation.
- **Loops** `{ t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]);` repeat a specification over an index, adding one term per occasion.
- **Definition variables** such as `d = ifelse(time < 1, 0, 1);` are expressions substituted into later equations; they are not new random variables.
- **Suffixes** `.lag` (lagged value of a variable) and `.mean` (latent person mean of a level-1 predictor) create derived variables that Blimp imputes alongside the data.

# Setup

## Load Packages

```{r packages}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(rblimp)
```

```{r blimp-path, include=FALSE}
# local Blimp build used for the knit; not shown in the rendered document
set_blimp('/applications/blimp/blimp-nightly')
```

## Read Data

```{r load-data}
github <- 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/craigenders/mnar-mlm/main/'

growth_dropout         <- read.csv(paste0(github, 'data/growth-dropout.csv'),         stringsAsFactors = T)
growth_intermittent    <- read.csv(paste0(github, 'data/growth-intermittent.csv'),    stringsAsFactors = T)
intensive_dropout      <- read.csv(paste0(github, 'data/intensive-dropout.csv'),      stringsAsFactors = T)
intensive_intermittent <- read.csv(paste0(github, 'data/intensive-intermittent.csv'), stringsAsFactors = T)
```

## Plotting Functions

```{r source-functions}
source('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/blimp-stats/blimp-book/main/misc/functions.R')
source('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/craigenders/mnar-mlm/main/rblimp/mnar-plotting.R')
```

The second file defines `plot_means()`, which draws averages of any variable in an `rblimp` model's imputed data by occasion and, optionally, by group. It is used throughout the tutorial for the missingness-probability figures and for the model-implied growth curves.

```r
plot_means(outcome ~ x_var | group_var, model = fit, ylab = , title = , group_labels = ,
           use_latent_growth = FALSE)
```

- `outcome` is any column of `fit@average_imp` (the imputed data averaged over iterations): an observed or imputed variable such as `m`, or a model-generated quantity such as `m.1.probability` (the predicted probability that `m` = 1).
- `x_var` is the horizontal axis (here `time`); `| group_var` is optional and draws one line per group.
- `use_latent_growth = TRUE` ignores `outcome` and instead draws strictly linear trajectories from each person's posterior random intercept and slope (`alpha.latent`, `beta.latent`), which is how the CMAR growth curves in Figure 1A are produced.
- The result is a `ggplot` object, so axis limits, themes, and line styles can be added with `+` as in the chunks below, and `patchwork` operators (`|`, `/`) arrange several plots.

## Helper Functions

The functions below extract parameter estimates and convergence diagnostics from `rblimp` model objects for the summary tables at the end of the tutorial.

```{r helper-functions, class.source="fold-hide"}
# function to extract key parameter estimates (growth model examples)
extract_growth_params <- function(object, method) {

  tab <- object@estimates

  rows <- c(
    "alpha ~ Intercept",
    "beta ~ Intercept",
    "alpha ~ group",
    "beta ~ group",
    "alpha residual variance",
    "beta residual variance",
    "Cor( alpha, beta )",
    "y residual variance",
    "Parameter: diff",
    "Parameter: d_diff",
    "m R2: Coefficients"
  )

  res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rows, function(r) {
    if (r %in% rownames(tab)) {
      round(tab[r, c("Estimate", "StdDev"), drop = FALSE], 2)
    } else {
      data.frame(Estimate = NA_real_, StdDev = NA_real_, row.names = r)
    }
  }))

  rownames(res) <- c(
    "Icept (G = 0)",
    "Slope (G = 0)",
    "Icept Diff.",
    "Slope Diff.",
    "Var(Icept)",
    "Var(Slope)",
    "Cor(Icept, Slope)",
    "Var(Residual)",
    "Mean Diff.",
    "Std. Diff.",
    "Pseudo-Rsq"
  )

  colnames(res) <- c(
    paste0("Est_", method),
    paste0("SE_", method)
  )

  res
}

# function to extract key parameter estimates (intensive longitudinal examples)
extract_intensive_params <- function(object, method) {

  tab <- object@estimates

  rows <- c(
    "alpha ~ Intercept",
    "beta ~ Intercept",
    "alpha ~ group",
    "beta ~ group",
    "alpha residual variance",
    "beta residual variance",
    "Cor( alpha, beta )",
    "y Variance Q50%",
    "omega ~ Intercept",
    "omega residual variance",
    "Cor( alpha, omega )",
    "Cor( beta, omega )",
    "Parameter: diff",
    "Parameter: d_diff",
    "m R2: Coefficients"
  )

  res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rows, function(r) {
    if (r %in% rownames(tab)) {
      round(tab[r, c("Estimate", "StdDev"), drop = FALSE], 2)
    } else {
      data.frame(Estimate = NA_real_, StdDev = NA_real_, row.names = r)
    }
  }))

  rownames(res) <- c(
    "Icept (G = 0)",
    "Slope (G = 0)",
    "Icept Diff.",
    "Slope Diff.",
    "Var(Icept)",
    "Var(Slope)",
    "Cor(Icept, Slope)",
    "Var(Residual)",
    "Icept Log-Var",
    "Var(Log-Var)",
    "Cor(Icept, Log-Var)",
    "Cor(Log-Var, Slope)",
    "Mean Diff.",
    "Std. Diff.",
    "Pseudo-Rsq"
  )

  colnames(res) <- c(
    paste0("Est_", method),
    paste0("SE_", method)
  )

  res
}

# function to extract convergence diagnostics
extract_convergence <- function(object, method) {

  neff <- object@estimates[, "N_Eff"]
  neff <- neff[is.finite(neff)]

  psr_row <- as.numeric(object@psr[20, ])
  psr_row <- psr_row[is.finite(psr_row)]

  data.frame(
    Min_Neff = round(min(neff),    3),
    Max_Neff = round(max(neff),    3),
    Min_PSR  = round(min(psr_row), 3),
    Max_PSR  = round(max(psr_row), 3),
    row.names = method
  )
}

# intraclass correlation of the latent missingness propensity
# (random intercept variance over the random intercept variance plus the fixed unit within-person variance)
icc_latent <- function(object) {
  tab  <- object@estimates
  rows <- rownames(tab)
  # random intercept variance of the missingness indicator m
  row  <- grep("^m .*(intercept|random).*var", rows, ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)
  if (length(row) == 0) {
    message("Random intercept variance row not found; candidate rows:")
    print(grep("^m ", rows, value = TRUE))
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  v <- tab[row[1], "Estimate"]
  round(v / (v + 1), 3)
}
```

# CMAR Models

The Appendix of the paper gives Blimp scripts for the two focal models under the conditionally missing at random (CMAR) assumption. These are the baselines against which every MNAR model is compared. The scripts below differ from the Appendix in two ways. First, they add a `PARAMETERS` command that computes the effect sizes reported in the paper's tables; the [Sensitivity Analysis Results](#sensitivity-analysis-results) section defines them. Second, they include the `TIMEID` and `DROPOUT` commands even though no missingness model is specified. By default Blimp analyzes every row of the data file, imputing the outcome at every missing occasion, whereas the `DROPOUT` command with the `(monotone)` keyword removes a person's rows after the dropout occasion. Including the command in the CMAR model ensures that the baseline and the MNAR models analyze the same rows, so that their estimates, standard errors, and effect sizes are directly comparable. With the `(missing)` keyword no rows are removed, but the command is retained in the intermittent examples so that all four baselines are specified in parallel.

## Growth Model

The growth model is fit to the dropout and intermittent data sets. The script is identical apart from the data file.

*Command by command:*

- `CLUSTERID: l2id;` identifies the person-level grouping variable.
- `TIMEID: time;` and `DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);` create the dropout indicator and restrict the analysis to the rows the MNAR models will use (see above). The indicator `m` is created but not modeled here.
- `LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;` declares the random intercept and slope as level-2 latent variables.
- `FIXED: group time;` declares the completely observed predictors so Blimp does not build distributional models for them.
- The `level2:` block regresses the random effects on `group`; the labels `@g0a`, `@g1a`, `@g0b`, `@g1b` name the four coefficients for use in `PARAMETERS`. `alpha ~~ beta;` estimates their covariance.
- The `level1:` block is the growth curve. `intercept@alpha` and `time@beta` assign the random effects to the intercept and slope.
- `PARAMETERS` defines `diff`, the mean difference between groups at the final occasion (*TIME* = 4), and `d_diff`, that difference standardized by the baseline standard deviation (the square root of the total random intercept variance plus the total within-person residual variance).

### Growth Data With Dropout (Model 1)

The first fit uses the growth data with dropout.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-dropout.csv;                               # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                            # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                        # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                           # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);                              # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;                              # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: group time;                                      # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                      # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                       # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                        # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                        # level-1 (focal) model
PARAMETERS:                                             # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                                            # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                            # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                            # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r model1-gd, cache=TRUE}
model1_gd <- rblimp(
  data = growth_dropout,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (monotone)',
  latent = 'l2id = alpha beta',
  fixed = 'group time',
  model = '
    level2:
    alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;
    beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;
    alpha ~~ beta;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;',
  parameters = '
    diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
    d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(model1_gd)
```

## Intensive Repeated Measures Model

The intensive model adds a time-varying covariate and a random within-person variance.

*Command by command:*

- `LATENT: l2id = alpha beta omega;` adds `omega`, the level-2 latent variable for each person's log residual variance.
- `CENTER: groupmean = x;` centers `x` at its latent person mean, so `beta` is a pure within-person slope. Blimp estimates the person means and imputes missing `x` values from an automatically generated background model.
- `omega ~ intercept@g0o;` is the level-2 equation for the log-variance; `alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;` estimates all three covariances.
- `var(y) ~ intercept@omega;` assigns the random log-variance to the level-1 residual variance (a location-scale model).
- `PARAMETERS` defines `diff` as the conditional mean difference at *X* = 0 (which is `g1a`, the group effect on the intercept) and `d_diff` as that difference divided by the square root of the total random intercept variance.

### Intensive Data With Dropout (Model 1)

The intensive model applied to the data with dropout.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: intensive-dropout.csv;             # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                             # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                         # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                            # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);               # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta omega;         # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: group time;                       # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
CENTER: groupmean = x;                   # latent group-mean centering of the level-1 covariate
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;       # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;        # random slope equation
  omega ~ intercept@g0o;                 # log-variance equation
  alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;  # random effect covariances
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;            # level-1 (focal) model
  var(y) ~ intercept@omega;              # within-person log-variance model
PARAMETERS:                              # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = g1a;
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                             # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                             # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                             # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r model1-id, cache=TRUE}
model1_id <- rblimp(
  data = intensive_dropout,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (monotone)',
  latent = 'l2id = alpha beta omega',
  fixed = 'group time',
  center = 'groupmean = x',
  model = '
    level2:
    alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;
    beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;
    omega ~ intercept@g0o;
    alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;
    var(y) ~ intercept@omega;',
  parameters = '
    diff = g1a;
    d_diff = diff / sqrt(alpha.totalvar);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(model1_id)
```

### Intensive Data With Intermittent Missingness (Model 1)

The same model applied to the intensive data with intermittent missingness.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: intensive-intermittent.csv;        # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                             # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                         # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                            # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (missing);                # missingness indicator (intermittent)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta omega;         # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: group time;                       # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
CENTER: groupmean = x;                   # latent group-mean centering of the level-1 covariate
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;       # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;        # random slope equation
  omega ~ intercept@g0o;                 # log-variance equation
  alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;  # random effect covariances
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;            # level-1 (focal) model
  var(y) ~ intercept@omega;              # within-person log-variance model
PARAMETERS:                              # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = g1a;
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                             # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                             # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                             # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r model1-ii, cache=TRUE}
model1_ii <- rblimp(
  data = intensive_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  latent = 'l2id = alpha beta omega',
  fixed = 'group time',
  center = 'groupmean = x',
  model = '
    level2:
    alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;
    beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;
    omega ~ intercept@g0o;
    alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;
    var(y) ~ intercept@omega;',
  parameters = '
    diff = g1a;
    d_diff = diff / sqrt(alpha.totalvar);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(model1_ii)
```

## Model-Implied Trajectories (Figure 1)

Figure 1 in the paper shows the group-specific regression lines from the CMAR models: linear growth trajectories for the growth data (Panel A) and simple slopes of the outcome on the within-person covariate for the intensive data (Panel B). Both are reproduced here from the Model 1 fits.

For the growth data, `plot_means()` with `use_latent_growth = TRUE` averages each person's posterior random intercept and slope within group and draws the implied lines.

```{r figure1a}
p_growth_d <- plot_means(y ~ time | group, model = model1_gd,
    ylab = "Y", title = "Growth Data With Dropout",
    group_labels = c("0" = "0", "1" = "1"), use_latent_growth = TRUE) + ylim(0, 7) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid"))

p_growth_i <- plot_means(y ~ time | group, model = model1_gi,
    ylab = "Y", title = "Growth Data With Intermittent Missingness",
    group_labels = c("0" = "0", "1" = "1"), use_latent_growth = TRUE) + ylim(0, 7) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid"))

p_growth_d | p_growth_i
```

For the intensive data, the simple slopes come directly from the level-2 estimates: the group-specific intercept is $\gamma_{0\alpha} + \gamma_{1\alpha}(\mathit{GROUP})$ and the group-specific slope is $\gamma_{0\beta} + \gamma_{1\beta}(\mathit{GROUP})$, evaluated over the range of the within-person covariate $X^{w}$ (centered, so 0 is a person's own mean). The helper below extracts the four coefficients from a fitted model and draws the lines.

```{r figure1b}
plot_simple_slopes <- function(model, xrange = c(-2, 2), title = NULL, ylab = "Y") {
  est <- model@estimates[, "Estimate"]
  g0a <- est["alpha ~ Intercept"]; g1a <- est["alpha ~ group"]
  g0b <- est["beta ~ Intercept"];  g1b <- est["beta ~ group"]
  xw  <- seq(xrange[1], xrange[2], length.out = 50)
  dat <- rbind(data.frame(xw = xw, group = "0", y = g0a + g0b * xw),
               data.frame(xw = xw, group = "1", y = (g0a + g1a) + (g0b + g1b) * xw))
  ggplot(dat, aes(x = xw, y = y, linetype = group)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("0" = "dashed", "1" = "solid")) +
    labs(title = title, x = "X (within-person centered)", y = ylab, linetype = "group") +
    theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
          legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center")
}

p_int_d <- plot_simple_slopes(model1_id, title = "Intensive Data With Dropout")
p_int_i <- plot_simple_slopes(model1_ii, title = "Intensive Data With Intermittent Missingness")

p_int_d | p_int_i
```

The same two functions can be applied to any of the MNAR fits below (for example, `plot_means(y ~ time | group, model = model2_gd, use_latent_growth = TRUE)`) to see how a missingness assumption changes the model-implied trajectories.

## Reading the Output

The table below describes each section of the `rblimp` output in the
order it appears. Detailed descriptions of the potential scale reduction
(PSR) convergence diagnostic, the model summary tables, and the
effective sample size autocorrelation diagnostic follow the table.

| Output Section                      | Description                                                                                                                    |
|:------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `BURN-IN POTENTIAL SCALE REDUCTION (PSR) OUTPUT`   | Assesses whether the MCMC warm-up period is sufficiently long; see detailed description below                                  |
| `DATA INFORMATION`                  | Gives information about the sample size and missing data rates                                                                 |
| `MODEL INFORMATION`                 | Reports the number of parameters and summarizes the fitted regression equations                                                |
| `MODEL FIT`                         | Reports DIC and WAIC and custom Wald tests, if specified                                                                       |
| `IMPUTED DATA SUMMARIES`            | Reports summary statistics for every manifest and latent variable in the model                                                 |
| `CORRELATIONS AMONG RESIDUALS`      | Reports correlations between pairs of residuals for a model's outcome variables                                                |
| `OUTCOME MODEL ESTIMATES`           | Parameter estimates, standard errors, credible intervals, and diagnostics; see detailed description below                      |
| `GENERATED PARAMETERS`              | Displays auxiliary parameters that are a function of the estimated parameters (e.g., mean difference, standardized mean difference) |

### PSR Convergence Diagnostic

The potential scale reduction factor (PSRF) or Rhat convergence
diagnostic appears near the top of the output. The PSRF assesses
whether the MCMC warm-up period is sufficiently long for the algorithm
to converge, which occurs when independent chains produce similar
parameter estimates. Smaller values closer to the theoretical minimum
of 1 are better, and values below 1.05 (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010) or
1.10 (Gelman et al., 2014) are generally considered adequate. The
"Highest PSR" column displays the highest (worst) value across all
model parameters. This value should be less than 1.05 (or 1.10) by the
end of the burn-in period (the final row of the table). If the highest
PSRF is too large, increase the number of burn-in iterations (specified
using the `burn` argument).

```
BURN-IN RHAT CONVERGENCE DIAGNOSTIC OUTPUT:

  NOTE: Rank-normalized Rhat (Vehtari et al., 2021) is being used.
        This applies rank normalization and chain folding for robust
        convergence detection across all chains.

  Comparing iterations across 4 chains    Highest Rhat   Parameter #
                           626 to 1250           1.035            15
                          1251 to 2500           1.016            16
                          1876 to 3750           1.007             8
                          2501 to 5000           1.007            16
                          3126 to 6250           1.005            15
                          3751 to 7500           1.006             1
                          4376 to 8750           1.007            16
                          5001 to 10000          1.008            16
                          5626 to 11250          1.003            15
                          6251 to 12500          1.003            15
                          6876 to 13750          1.004            15
                          7501 to 15000          1.004            16
                          8126 to 16250          1.004            15
                          8751 to 17500          1.003             1
                          9376 to 18750          1.005             1
                         10001 to 20000          1.003             1
                         10626 to 21250          1.002            16
                         11251 to 22500          1.003            16
                         11876 to 23750          1.004            16
                         12501 to 25000          1.004             1
```

### Outcome Model Estimates

Each outcome variable has its own summary table containing raw and
standardized coefficients, variances and standard deviations, and
variance explained effect sizes. The Estimate column gives the point
estimates (posterior median), the StdDev column displays "Bayesian
standard errors" (posterior standard deviations), the 2.5% and 97.5%
columns display 95% credible intervals. The ChiSq and PValue columns
are frequentist significance tests (Wald chi-square values).

```
Latent Variable:   alpha

Parameters                         Estimate   StdDev     2.5%    97.5%       ChiSq  PValue     N_Eff
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Variances:
  Residual Var.                       0.330    0.055    0.227    0.442         ---     ---   1405.347

Coefficients:
  Intercept                           6.338    0.059    6.221    6.451   11671.323   0.000   5757.221
  group                               0.019    0.079   -0.134    0.178       0.059   0.809   5251.418

Standard Deviations:
  Residual SD                         0.575    0.048    0.476    0.665         ---     ---   1368.148

Standardized Coefficients:
  group                               0.017    0.069   -0.116    0.153       0.058   0.810   5223.293

Proportion Variance Explained
  by Coefficients                     0.002    0.007    0.000    0.025         ---     ---   9066.038
  by Residual Variation               0.998    0.007    0.975    1.000         ---     ---   9066.038

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

The tables for alpha (random intercept) and beta (random slope)
summarize the focal model's level-2 regression equations and random
coefficient variation. The intensive longitudinal examples add a table
for omega (random within-person log-variation). The table for y displays
the level-1 (within-person) residual variance.

The table for m displays the missingness model parameters. The
missingness model's pseudo-R2 (the proportion of variance explained on
the latent response metric) is often the clearest indicator of model
quality. Values around .70 or higher suggest that the predictors almost
perfectly classify dropouts from completers, a condition known as
near-separation. Very large effect sizes almost always signal that a
model lacks support from the data.

### N_Eff Diagnostic

The rightmost column in the parameter summary tables labeled N_Eff is
the effective sample size (ESS) diagnostic. The ESS provides a gauge of
whether the post-warm-up parameter summaries have sufficient precision.
Numerically, it reflects the effective number of MCMC iterations (the
"sample size") that contribute to these summaries after accounting for
autocorrelation in the sampling process. Larger values are better, and
values above 100 are generally considered adequate (Gelman et al., 2014,
p. 287). Inadequate PSRF and ESS values indicate that more iterations
are needed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Missing Data Indicators

MNAR analyses require a secondary model with a level-1 binary missing data indicator *M* as the outcome of a probit regression. The coding of *M* depends on whether missing data patterns reflect intermittent missingness, attrition, or both (Table 1 in the paper).

**Intermittent missingness** requires a generic indicator that codes whether the outcome is missing at occasion *t* (*M* = 1 if missing, 0 otherwise). Two commands added to a CMAR script create it:

```
TIMEID: time;                 # occasion index
DROPOUT: m = y (missing);     # m = 1 where y is missing, 0 otherwise
```

**Monotone dropout** requires an indicator that signals attrition: all occasions before dropout equal 0, the first missing occasion equals 1, and all later occasions are `NA` (those rows carry no information). The model-predicted probabilities are then the conditional probability of leaving at occasion *t* given participation at *t* -- 1, matching hazard probabilities in discrete-time survival models.

```
TIMEID: time;                 # occasion index
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);    # m = 1 at the first missing occasion, NA afterward
```

In `rblimp` these become `timeid = 'time'` and `dropout = 'm = y (missing)'` or `dropout = 'm = y (monotone)'`. Every model in this tutorial, including the CMAR baselines, carries one of these pairs; the CMAR section explains why. Blimp sorts the data by cluster and time and inserts rows for any occasions that are absent from the file, so lagged variables and the dropout indicator are correctly aligned even when the input data are not time-balanced.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Modeling Time Trends in Missingness

The validity of any MNAR model hinges on correctly specifying the missingness process. Although that assumption cannot be verified, the missingness model should at least reproduce the observed pattern of missing data rates over time: the latent curve SEMs do so automatically through occasion-specific intercepts, and conditioning on time strengthens the CMAR portion of the model before MNAR terms are added. In stacked data there are two strategies, polynomial functions of time and dummy-coded occasions, and the sections below evaluate both with graphical diagnostics. Following the paper, intermittent missingness is treated first because the dropout models are obtained by fixing or removing parameters from the intermittent specification.

Every model in this section pairs the focal CMAR model with a `missingness:` block. The focal model is unchanged from the CMAR scripts above and is estimated jointly with the missingness model; only the missingness block is new.

## Intermittent Missingness

Intermittent patterns have missing values at every occasion, so the stacked vector of indicators can be partitioned into a between-person component (a person's overall propensity for missingness) and within-person deviations from it. The recommended starting point is an empty random intercept model that quantifies the two sources.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + u_i + z_{ti}, \qquad u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_u), \quad z_{ti} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad \tau = 0$$

Fixing the threshold at 0 and the within-person variance at 1 identifies the model. The intraclass correlation of the latent response, $\sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + 1)$, is the proportion of variation in missingness propensity that is between persons. The scripts below fit only the missingness model (no focal model is needed for this step).

*Important features of the specification:*

- `m ~ intercept | intercept;` regresses the indicator on a fixed intercept, with a random intercept after the vertical pipe.
- The focal model is omitted, so `LATENT` and `FIXED` are not needed.

### Growth Data

The empty model for the growth data with intermittent missingness.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-intermittent.csv;     # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                       # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                   # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                      # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (missing);          # missingness indicator (intermittent)
MODEL: m ~ intercept | intercept;
SEED: 90291;                       # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                       # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                       # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r icc-gi, cache=TRUE}
icc_gi <- rblimp(
  data = growth_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  model = 'm ~ intercept | intercept;',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(icc_gi)
```

```{r icc-gi-value}
icc_latent(icc_gi)
```

### Polynomial and Dummy-Coded Time: Growth Data

The linear model adds a temporal predictor (*TIME* = 0, 1, ..., *T* -- 1), the grouping variable, and their interaction.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \lambda_1(\mathit{GROUP}_i) + \lambda_2(\mathit{TIME}_{ti}) + \lambda_3(\mathit{GROUP}_i)(\mathit{TIME}_{ti}) + u_i + z_{ti}$$

On the probability scale, $\lambda_0$ is the baseline missingness rate for *GROUP* = 0, $\lambda_1$ the group difference at baseline, $\lambda_2$ the monotonic change over time for *GROUP* = 0, and $\lambda_3$ the group difference in that change. Because the probit link is S-shaped, a linear model can only produce concave-up probability curves while probabilities stay below .50; the quadratic model relaxes that. The dummy-coded model instead includes *T* -- 1 occasion dummy codes and their products with group, reproducing any temporal pattern.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \lambda_1(\mathit{GROUP}_i) + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left[\lambda_{t0}(O_{ti}) + \lambda_{t1}(O_{ti})(\mathit{GROUP}_i)\right] + u_i + z_{ti}$$

*Important features of the specifications:*

- The three models differ only in the `missingness:` block; the `level2:` and `level1:` blocks are the CMAR growth model.
- `time^2` is the squared occasion index.
- In the dummy-coded model, `{ t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;` loops over occasions 1 through 4, adding a Boolean dummy code `(time == t)` and its product with `group` at each pass. This is equivalent to writing out eight terms by hand and mimics the summation in the equation.

#### Linear Time



**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-intermittent.csv;                      # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                        # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                    # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                       # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (missing);                           # missingness indicator (intermittent)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;                          # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: time group;                                  # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                  # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                   # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                    # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                    # level-1 (focal) model
  missingness:
  m ~ intercept time group time*group | intercept;  # missingness model
SEED: 90291;                                        # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                        # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                        # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r time-linear-gi, cache=TRUE}
time_linear_gi <- rblimp(
  data = growth_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  latent = 'l2id = alpha beta',
  fixed = 'time group',
  model = '
    level2:
    alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;
    beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;
    alpha ~~ beta;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;
    missingness:
    m ~ intercept time group time*group | intercept;',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(time_linear_gi)
```

#### Quadratic Time



**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-intermittent.csv;                                          # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                                            # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                                        # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                                           # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (missing);                                               # missingness indicator (intermittent)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;                                              # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: time group;                                                      # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ 1 group;                                                      # random intercept equation
  beta ~ 1 group;                                                       # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                                        # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                                        # level-1 (focal) model
  missingness:
  m ~ intercept time time^2 group time*group time^2*group | intercept;  # missingness model
SEED: 90291;                                                            # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                                            # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                                            # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r time-quadratic-gi, cache=TRUE}
time_quadratic_gi <- rblimp(
  data = growth_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  latent = 'l2id = alpha beta',
  fixed = 'time group',
  model = '
    level2:
    alpha ~ 1 group;
    beta ~ 1 group;
    alpha ~~ beta;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;
    missingness:
    m ~ intercept time time^2 group time*group time^2*group | intercept;',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(time_quadratic_gi)
```

#### Dummy-Coded Time



**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-intermittent.csv;                           # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                             # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                         # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                            # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (missing);                                # missingness indicator (intermittent)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;                               # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: time group;                                       # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                       # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                        # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                         # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                         # level-1 (focal) model
  missingness:
  m ~ intercept group | intercept;                       # missingness model
  { t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;  # loop adds occasion dummy codes
PARAMETERS:                                              # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                                             # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                             # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                             # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r time-dummy-gi, cache=TRUE}
time_dummy_gi <- rblimp(
  data = growth_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  latent = 'l2id = alpha beta',
  fixed = 'time group',
  model = '
    level2:
    alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;
    beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;
    alpha ~~ beta;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;
    missingness:
    m ~ intercept group | intercept;
    { t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;',
  parameters = '
    diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
    d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(time_dummy_gi)
```

#### Observed and Predicted Probabilities

The plots compare the observed occasion-specific missing data rates by group with the average individual predicted probabilities from each model (Figure 3, left column, in the paper).

```{r miss-plots-gi}
ymin <- 0
ymax <- .35

plot_pmiss_obs_gi <- plot_means(m ~ time | group, model = time_dummy_gi,
    ylab = "Probability", title = "Observed Probabilities",
    group_labels = c("0" = "0", "1" = "1")) + ylim(ymin, ymax) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid")) + geom_line(linewidth = .25)

plot_pmiss_linear_gi <- plot_means(m.1.probability ~ time | group, model = time_linear_gi,
    ylab = "Probability", title = "Linear Time",
    group_labels = c("0" = "0", "1" = "1")) + ylim(ymin, ymax) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid")) + geom_line(linewidth = .25)

plot_pmiss_quadratic_gi <- plot_means(m.1.probability ~ time | group, model = time_quadratic_gi,
    ylab = "Probability", title = "Quadratic Time",
    group_labels = c("0" = "0", "1" = "1")) + ylim(ymin, ymax) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid")) + geom_line(linewidth = .25)

plot_pmiss_dummy_gi <- plot_means(m.1.probability ~ time | group, model = time_dummy_gi,
    ylab = "Probability", title = "Dummy-Coded Time",
    group_labels = c("0" = "0", "1" = "1")) + ylim(ymin, ymax) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid")) + geom_line(linewidth = .25)

(plot_pmiss_obs_gi | plot_pmiss_linear_gi) / (plot_pmiss_quadratic_gi | plot_pmiss_dummy_gi)
```

The table compares the observed probabilities with the average model-predicted probabilities from each specification (RMSE and the minimum, median, mean, and maximum occasion-specific discrepancy).

```{r miss-fit-gi, class.source="fold-hide"}
pmiss_obs       <- aggregate(m ~ time + group,               data = time_dummy_gi@average_imp,     mean)
pmiss_linear    <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_linear_gi@average_imp,    mean)
pmiss_quadratic <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_quadratic_gi@average_imp, mean)
pmiss_dummy     <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_dummy_gi@average_imp,     mean)

dev <- list(Linear    = pmiss_linear$m.1.probability    - pmiss_obs$m,
            Quadratic = pmiss_quadratic$m.1.probability - pmiss_obs$m,
            Dummy     = pmiss_dummy$m.1.probability     - pmiss_obs$m)

miss_fit_gi <- data.frame(
  RMSE   = round(sapply(dev, function(x) sqrt(mean(x^2))), 3),
  Min    = round(sapply(dev, min), 3),
  Median = round(sapply(dev, median), 3),
  Mean   = round(sapply(dev, mean), 3),
  Max    = round(sapply(dev, max), 3))
knitr::kable(miss_fit_gi, caption = "Predicted Minus Observed Missingness Probabilities")
```

### Polynomial and Dummy-Coded Time: Intensive Data

The intensive data use the same three specifications. The only change is that the loop runs from *t* = 1 to 19. The dummy-coded model adds a `WALDTEST` command that jointly tests the occasion effects.

#### Linear Time



**Blimp script**

```
DATA: intensive-intermittent.csv;                   # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                        # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                    # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                       # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (missing);                           # missingness indicator (intermittent)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta omega;                    # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: time group;                                  # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
CENTER: groupmean = x;                              # latent group-mean centering of the level-1 covariate
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                  # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                   # random slope equation
  omega ~ intercept@g0o;                            # log-variance equation
  alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;             # random effect covariances
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;                       # level-1 (focal) model
  var(y) ~ intercept@omega;                         # within-person log-variance model
  missingness:
  m ~ intercept time group time*group | intercept;  # missingness model
SEED: 90291;                                        # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                        # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                        # analysis iterations
```

The table compares the observed probabilities with the average model-predicted probabilities from each specification (RMSE and the minimum, median, mean, and maximum occasion-specific discrepancy).

```{r miss-fit-ii, class.source="fold-hide"}
pmiss_obs       <- aggregate(m ~ time + group,               data = time_dummy_ii@average_imp,     mean)
pmiss_linear    <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_linear_ii@average_imp,    mean)
pmiss_quadratic <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_quadratic_ii@average_imp, mean)
pmiss_dummy     <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_dummy_ii@average_imp,     mean)

dev <- list(Linear    = pmiss_linear$m.1.probability    - pmiss_obs$m,
            Quadratic = pmiss_quadratic$m.1.probability - pmiss_obs$m,
            Dummy     = pmiss_dummy$m.1.probability     - pmiss_obs$m)

miss_fit_ii <- data.frame(
  RMSE   = round(sapply(dev, function(x) sqrt(mean(x^2))), 3),
  Min    = round(sapply(dev, min), 3),
  Median = round(sapply(dev, median), 3),
  Mean   = round(sapply(dev, mean), 3),
  Max    = round(sapply(dev, max), 3))
knitr::kable(miss_fit_ii, caption = "Predicted Minus Observed Missingness Probabilities")
```

### Equivalence With IRT Missingness Models

Dummy coding is equivalent to the one- and two-parameter IRT missingness models of Cursio et al. (2019). After removing group effects, the dummy-coded model is a one-parameter IRT model in which the random intercept is the latent propensity and the occasion dummy codes are item difficulties; adding cross-level interactions between the random intercept and the dummy codes gives the two-parameter model with occasion-specific discriminations. The companion document *Dummy-Coded Missingness Models and Their IRT Equivalents* in the repository gives the algebra and fits both models to the intensive data.

## Dropout

Monotone patterns differ from intermittent patterns in two ways. Each person's dropout vector contains at most one *M* = 1, so there is no within-person variation to support a random intercept, and dropout can only occur after the first measurement. The dropout models therefore omit the random intercept (`| intercept@0`) and the baseline group effect, and they fix the fixed intercept at a value that yields a near-zero probability at baseline: `intercept@-3` gives $\Phi(-3) \approx .0014$ and supports stable estimation. Latent curve SEMs achieve the same thing by omitting the baseline indicator.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \lambda_1(\mathit{TIME}_{ti}) + \lambda_2(\mathit{GROUP}_i)(\mathit{TIME}_{ti}) + z_{ti}$$

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left[\lambda_{t0}(O_{ti}) + \lambda_{t1}(O_{ti})(\mathit{GROUP}_i)\right] + z_{ti}$$

*Important features of the specifications:*

- `dropout = 'm = y (monotone)'` creates the attrition indicator.
- `intercept@-3` fixes the fixed intercept; `| intercept@0` fixes the random intercept variance to zero. The `@` symbol fixes a parameter at the value that follows it.
- The group main effect is omitted because it is not estimable at baseline, where nobody has dropped out.

### Polynomial and Dummy-Coded Time: Intensive Data

In the intensive data the first seven occasions are complete, so dropout rates jump from zero at *t* = 7. Modeling this requires a dummy variable *D* that equals 0 before *t* = 7 and 1 thereafter; products with *D* switch the time effects on at occasions where dropout can occur.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left[\lambda_{t0}(O_{ti})(D_{ti}) + \lambda_{t1}(O_{ti})(\mathit{GROUP}_i)(D_{ti})\right] + z_{ti}$$

*Important features of the specifications:*

- `d = ifelse(time < 7, 0, 1);` is a definition variable: an expression substituted into the equations that follow, not a new random variable.
- In the polynomial models, `(time - 7)` restarts the time index at the switch point, and every term is multiplied by `d`.
- In the dummy-coded model, the loop runs from 1 to 19 but every dummy code is multiplied by `d`, so occasions 1--6 contribute nothing.
- `nimps = 20` in the polynomial models saves 20 imputed data sets; the other scripts rely on the default. The plotting function averages the saved predicted probabilities either way.

#### Linear Time



**Blimp script**

```
DATA: intensive-dropout.csv;                                                 # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                                                 # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                                             # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                                                # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);                                                   # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta omega;                                             # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: time group;                                                           # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
CENTER: groupmean = x;                                                       # latent group-mean centering of the level-1 covariate
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                                           # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                                            # random slope equation
  omega ~ intercept@g0o;                                                     # log-variance equation
  alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;                                      # random effect covariances
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;                                                # level-1 (focal) model
  var(y) ~ intercept@omega;                                                  # within-person log-variance model
  missingness:
  d = ifelse(time < 7, 0, 1);                                                # definition variable: switch dummy code
  m ~ intercept@-3 d group*d (time - 7)*d (time - 7)*group*d | intercept@0;  # missingness model
SEED: 90291;                                                                 # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                                                 # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                                                 # analysis iterations
NIMPS: 20;                                                                   # imputations saved for plotting
```

```{r time-quadratic-id, cache=TRUE}
    level2:
    alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;
    beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;
    omega ~ intercept@g0o;
    alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;
    var(y) ~ intercept@omega;
    missingness:
    d = ifelse(time < 7, 0, 1);
    m ~ intercept@-3 d group*d (time - 7)*d (time - 7)^2*d (time - 7)*group*d (time - 7)^2*group*d | intercept@0;',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000,
  nimps = 20)

output(time_quadratic_id)
```

#### Dummy-Coded Time



**Blimp script**

```
DATA: intensive-dropout.csv;                                  # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                                  # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                              # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                                 # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);                                    # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta omega;                              # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: time group;                                            # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
CENTER: groupmean = x;                                        # latent group-mean centering of the level-1 covariate
MODEL:

  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                            # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                             # random slope equation
  omega ~ intercept@g0o;                                      # log-variance equation
  alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;                       # random effect covariances

  m ~ intercept@-3 | intercept@0;                             # missingness model

SEED: 90291;                                                  # random number seed
```

The table compares the observed probabilities with the average model-predicted probabilities from each specification (RMSE and the minimum, median, mean, and maximum occasion-specific discrepancy).

```{r miss-fit-id, class.source="fold-hide"}
pmiss_obs       <- aggregate(m ~ time + group,               data = time_dummy_id@average_imp,     mean)
pmiss_linear    <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_linear_id@average_imp,    mean)
pmiss_quadratic <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_quadratic_id@average_imp, mean)
pmiss_dummy     <- aggregate(m.1.probability ~ time + group, data = time_dummy_id@average_imp,     mean)

dev <- list(Linear    = pmiss_linear$m.1.probability    - pmiss_obs$m,
            Quadratic = pmiss_quadratic$m.1.probability - pmiss_obs$m,
            Dummy     = pmiss_dummy$m.1.probability     - pmiss_obs$m)

miss_fit_id <- data.frame(
  RMSE   = round(sapply(dev, function(x) sqrt(mean(x^2))), 3),
  Min    = round(sapply(dev, min), 3),
  Median = round(sapply(dev, median), 3),
  Mean   = round(sapply(dev, mean), 3),
  Max    = round(sapply(dev, max), 3))
knitr::kable(miss_fit_id, caption = "Predicted Minus Observed Missingness Probabilities")
```

# Shared Parameter Models

The defining feature of the Wu--Carroll (1988) shared parameter model is that the random effects of the focal model appear as predictors in the missingness model. Because the same latent variables drive both the outcome and nonresponse, they induce an association between *Y* and *M*. Any random effect in the focal model can play this role, which makes the model readily applicable to intensive repeated measures data. All models continue to use dummy-coded time. Results for every model are collected in the [Sensitivity Analysis Results](#sensitivity-analysis-results) section.

## Growth Data With Dropout

With attrition, the first occasion is structurally complete. The SEM omits the first dropout indicator; the MLM instead needs a time-varying dummy variable *D* (0 at baseline, 1 afterward) whose products with the random effects switch their influence on at occasions where dropout can occur.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left[\lambda_{t0}(O_{ti}) + \lambda_{t1}(O_{ti})(\mathit{GROUP}_i)\right] + \lambda_1(\alpha_i)(D_{ti}) + \lambda_2(\beta_i)(D_{ti}) + z_{ti}$$

The $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ terms induce the MNAR mechanism. The fixed intercept of --3 plays the role of omitting the baseline indicator, the occasion dummy codes allow occasion-specific dropout rates, and the interactions with *D* confine the random effects to post-baseline occasions, so the model is fully equivalent to the latent curve shared parameter model.

### Model 2: Random Effects Predicting Attrition

The missingness block adds the switched random effects to the dummy-coded dropout model from the previous section.

*Important features of the specification:*

- `d = ifelse(time < 1, 0, 1);` defines the switch (0 at baseline, 1 afterward).
- `alpha*d beta*d` are the random intercept and slope, activated after baseline.
- The `level2:` labels `@g0a`, `@g1a`, `@g0b`, `@g1b` are used by `PARAMETERS` and, in Model 4, by the residual definition variables.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-dropout.csv;                                # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                             # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                         # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                            # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);                               # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;                               # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: group time;                                       # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                       # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                        # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                         # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                         # level-1 (focal) model
  missingness:
  d = ifelse(time < 1, 0, 1);                            # definition variable: switch dummy code
  m ~ intercept@-3 alpha*d beta*d | intercept@0;         # missingness model
  { t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;  # loop adds occasion dummy codes
PARAMETERS:                                              # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                                             # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                             # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                             # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r model2-gd, cache=TRUE}

  data = growth_dropout,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',

  fixed = 'group time',

    alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;
    beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;
    alpha ~~ beta;
    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;
    missingness:
    d = ifelse(time < 1, 0, 1);
    m ~ intercept@-3 alpha*d beta*d | intercept@0;
    { t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;',
  parameters = '
    diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
    d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(model2_gd)
```

### Model 3: Random Effects and Their Squares Predicting Attrition

A linear specification lets only one tail of the random effect distribution predict higher nonresponse. Adding squared random effects allows attrition to depend on both tails (for example, both rapid improvers and non-responders disengaging). Nonlinear effects of latent variables are computationally demanding and may require larger samples.

*Important features of the specification:*

- `alpha*d^2` and `beta*d^2` are the squared random effects; because `d` is 0 or 1, `d^2 = d`, and the terms are the squares of `alpha` and `beta` activated after baseline.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-dropout.csv;                                            # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                                         # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                                     # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                                        # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);                                           # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;                                           # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: group time;                                                   # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                                   # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                                    # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                                     # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                                     # level-1 (focal) model
  missingness:
  d = ifelse(time < 1, 0, 1);                                        # definition variable: switch dummy code
  m ~ intercept@-3 alpha*d alpha*d^2 beta*d beta*d^2 | intercept@0;  # missingness model
  { t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;              # loop adds occasion dummy codes
PARAMETERS:                                                          # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                                                         # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                                         # warm-up iterations
ITER: 25000;                                                         # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

### Model 4: Random Effect Residuals Predicting Attrition

When the focal model includes predictors of the random effects, as it does here, `alpha` and `beta` in the missingness model are composites that include the group effect, so $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are not pure estimates of MNAR signal. The alternative uses the level-2 residuals, isolating the component of each random effect that is orthogonal to its predictors. The residuals are computed at every MCMC iteration from the current random effects and the current level-2 coefficients.

$$\zeta_{\alpha i} = \alpha_i - \left[\gamma_{0\alpha} + \gamma_{1\alpha}(\mathit{GROUP}_i)\right] \qquad \zeta_{\beta i} = \beta_i - \left[\gamma_{0\beta} + \gamma_{1\beta}(\mathit{GROUP}_i)\right]$$

*Important features of the specification:*

- `alpha_res = alpha - (g0a + g1a*group);` and `beta_res = ...` are definition variables that subtract the level-2 predicted values; the labels `g0a`, `g1a`, `g0b`, `g1b` refer to the coefficients named in the `level2:` block.
- This model needed 100,000 iterations to reach adequate diagnostics.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: growth-dropout.csv;                                 # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                              # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                          # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                             # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);                                # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta;                                # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: group time;                                        # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                        # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                         # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                          # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                          # level-1 (focal) model
  missingness:
  alpha_res = alpha - (g0a + g1a*group);                  # definition variable: intercept residual
  beta_res = beta - (g0b + g1b*group);                    # definition variable: slope residual
  d = ifelse(time < 1, 0, 1);                             # definition variable: switch dummy code
  m ~ intercept@-3 alpha_res*d beta_res*d | intercept@0;  # missingness model
  { t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;   # loop adds occasion dummy codes
PARAMETERS:                                               # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                                              # random number seed
BURN: 100000;                                             # warm-up iterations
ITER: 100000;                                             # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

## Growth Data With Intermittent Missingness

With missingness at every occasion, the random effects can influence nonresponse over the whole study, so no switch is needed. The fixed intercept is estimable, the group main effect returns, and a random intercept allows person-level missingness propensities to vary.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \lambda_1(\mathit{GROUP}_i) + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left[\lambda_{t0}(O_{ti}) + \lambda_{t1}(O_{ti})(\mathit{GROUP}_i)\right] + \lambda_2(\alpha_i) + \lambda_3(\beta_i) + u_i + z_{ti}$$

### Model 2: Random Effects Predicting Missingness

The missingness block adds `alpha` and `beta` to the dummy-coded intermittent model.

*Important features of the specification:*

- `m ~ intercept group alpha beta | intercept;` -- all parameters are free, including the random intercept after the pipe.

**Blimp script**

```

MISSING: NA;                                             # missing value code

MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                       # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                        # random slope equation
  alpha ~~ beta;                                         # random effect covariance
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha time@beta;                         # level-1 (focal) model
  missingness:
  m ~ intercept group alpha beta | intercept;            # missingness model
  { t in 1:4 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*group;  # loop adds occasion dummy codes
PARAMETERS:                                              # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                                             # random number seed
BURN: 25000;                                             # warm-up iterations
```

```{r model4-gi, cache=TRUE}
  parameters = '
    diff = (((g0a+g1a)  + 4*(g0b+g1b)) - (g0a + 4*g0b));
    d_diff = diff / sqrt(y.totalvar + alpha.totalvar);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(model4_gi)
```

## Intensive Data With Dropout

In a stationary intensive design it is less obvious which random effects belong in the missingness model. The random intercept is the stable component of a person's outcome (their average level) and is the natural first choice. Whether to include the random slope for a time-varying covariate is a substantive decision. The paper's examples instead use the log-variance random effect $\omega_i$, on the grounds that the magnitude of a person's intraindividual variability is itself a plausible determinant of nonresponse: two people with the same average level can differ in how much they fluctuate, and the one with larger swings may find the protocol harder to sustain.

Dropout begins after occasion 7, so *D* switches at *t* = 7, and the occasion dummy codes are also multiplied by *D* as in the time-trend models.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left[\lambda_{t0}(O_{ti})(D_{ti}) + \lambda_{t1}(O_{ti})(\mathit{GROUP}_i)(D_{ti})\right] + \lambda_1(\alpha_i)(D_{ti}) + \lambda_2(\omega_i)(D_{ti}) + z_{ti}$$

### Model 2: Random Effects Predicting Attrition

The random intercept and the log-variance random effect, activated after occasion 7.

*Important features of the specification:*

- `d = ifelse(time < 7, 0, 1);` switches at occasion 7.
- `alpha*d omega*d` are the random intercept and log-variance, activated by `d`.
- Both the random-effect terms and the dummy codes in the loop are multiplied by `d`.

**Blimp script**

```
DATA: intensive-dropout.csv;                                  # raw data file
MISSING: NA;                                                  # missing value code
CLUSTERID: l2id;                                              # level-2 identifier
TIMEID: time;                                                 # occasion index for lags and dropout coding
DROPOUT: m = y (monotone);                                    # dropout indicator (monotone)
LATENT: l2id = alpha beta omega;                              # level-2 latent variables (random effects)
FIXED: group time;                                            # complete predictors (speeds estimation)
CENTER: groupmean = x;                                        # latent group-mean centering of the level-1 covariate
MODEL:
  level2:
  alpha ~ intercept@g0a group@g1a;                            # random intercept equation
  beta ~ intercept@g0b group@g1b;                             # random slope equation
  omega ~ intercept@g0o;                                      # log-variance equation
  alpha beta omega ~~ alpha beta omega;                       # random effect covariances
  level1:
  y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;                                 # level-1 (focal) model
  var(y) ~ intercept@omega;                                   # within-person log-variance model
  missingness:
  d = ifelse(time < 7, 0, 1);                                 # definition variable: switch dummy code
  m ~ intercept@-3 alpha*d omega*d | intercept@0;             # missingness model
  { t in 1:19 } : m ~ (time == [t])*d (time == [t])*group*d;  # loop adds occasion dummy codes
PARAMETERS:                                                   # derived quantities (effect sizes)
  diff = g1a;
  d_diff = diff / sqrt(alpha.totalvar);
SEED: 90291;                                                  # random number seed
BURN: 75000;                                                  # warm-up iterations
ITER: 75000;                                                  # analysis iterations
```

**rblimp**

```{r model2-id, cache=TRUE}

    level1:
    y ~ intercept@alpha x@beta;
    var(y) ~ intercept@omega;

    d = ifelse(time < 7, 0, 1);
    m ~ intercept@-3 alpha*d omega*d | intercept@0;
    { t in 1:19 } : m ~ (time == [t])*d (time == [t])*group*d;',

    diff = g1a;
    d_diff = diff / sqrt(alpha.totalvar);',

  iter = 75000)

output(model2_id)
```

### Model 4: Random Effect Residuals Predicting Attrition

The random intercept residual replaces the raw random intercept. Because `omega` has no level-2 predictors, it is already a residual and enters as is.

### Model 5: Random Effects and *X* Latent Means Predicting Attrition

When both *X* and *Y* are missing at the same occasions, *M* indicates joint nonresponse. If the unseen *X* scores plausibly relate to attrition, the level-2 latent mean of *X* can be added as a shared parameter, so that nonresponse depends on the unobserved values of both variables. Blimp constructs a background model for *X* to estimate its person means and impute its missing values.

$$M^*_{ti} = \lambda_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left[\lambda_{t0}(O_{ti})(D_{ti}) + \lambda_{t1}(O_{ti})(\mathit{GROUP}_i)(D_{ti})\right] + \lambda_1(\alpha_i)(D_{ti}) + \lambda_2(\omega_i)(D_{ti}) + \lambda_3(\mu_{Xi})(D_{ti}) + z_{ti}$$

*Important features of the specification:*

- `x.mean` is the latent person mean of `x`, the same quantity used by `CENTER: groupmean = x`.
- This model reached the 200,000-iteration cap and is flagged as inadmissible in Table 4.

**Blimp script**

